How to use the simulator

1 · Quick start

  1. Click anywhere once so the browser allows alarm sound. Check the top bar shows 🔔 Sound on.
  2. The session opens at design: pump P-200A draws cat-cracker feed from tank T200 and delivers 14 L/s through FE-100 and V100 (FRC-100), the steam preheater E-100 and the feed drum D-150 to the cat cracker. P-200B is the identical spare, lined up with its suction and discharge valves open. Open P&ID to see the plant, Pump curves to see where the pump runs, then DCS console to operate it.
  3. Go to Exercises, pick a list (Training, Think EQUIPPED or Procedures) and click Load. A blue banner gives the situation; Acknowledge it to hide it.
  4. Operate from the DCS console: click an instrument bubble, a pump or a valve to open its faceplate. Pumps, hand valves, vents, the local gauges and the telephones are on the Field tab. The local gauges PI-209, PI-210 and PI-220 are not on the DCS: send the field operator to read them.
  5. Use Speed to run faster (2×–50×) and Freeze to pause while you think. Flows settle in seconds, temperatures in minutes, tank levels over tens of minutes.
  6. When finished, open Debrief and grading for your score, then Data export to download CSV files for your report.

ScoreContinuous score (starts at 100); see Debrief and grading.

4 · DCS console

  • Overview: FRC-100, V100, TIC-110 and steam; both motors (current and casing temperature); T200, D-150 and the cat-cracker charge; the SIS state.
  • Pumps: a motor table (state, current, power estimated from current, casing, speed) and a live pump-curve chart with the system curve at the present V100 opening and the expected operating point.
  • Preheater and D-150: heat balance of E-100 from measured values, TIC-110, and the D-150 level balance with time to low level.
  • Energy: pump electricity, steam and the cost of feed not delivered.

Instrument bubbles follow ISA style. A circle without a bar is a local instrument (no value on the DCS). A square frame marks a trip switch. Dashed brown bubbles PIT-210/220 appear only after the Rev C upgrade is installed on the SIS tab.

5 · Pump curves tab

  • Blue / green: test curves of A (shut-off 45.0 m) and B (46.5 m) at 3600 rpm; purple dotted: A + B in parallel; red: system curve at the present V100 opening, red dashed: V100 fully open.
  • Hollow circle: where the pump(s) should run if everything is healthy. Blue dashed line: what FRC-100 reads.
  • Gauge check: read PI-210 or PI-220 (and PI-209) on the Field tab; the square marks the measured head at the metered flow, and the line runs to the flow the test curve gives at that head. A big gap means flow is going somewhere else, the meter is wrong, or the pump is not healthy.
  • Calculator: move V100 opening, speed, static head, tank level or the pump combination; the orange curve and the table give the new flow. Use the plant now returns to live values.

PartWhat it does
ControllersPV, SP and OUT bars; Manual / Automatic (bumpless); SP and OUT fields; tuning. FRC-100 set point comes from the cat cracker (14 L/s).
PumpsSTART / STOP at the local station. A tripped motor will not restart until the trip is reset on the SIS tab.

7 · Trend and alarm summary

Trend groups: station overview, pumps, preheater, tanks, Rev C casing transmitters, or the selected tag. Alarm summary: newest unacknowledged first; click a row to acknowledge it and open that instrument.

8 · Safety system (SIS)

Reset clears a unit trip (T200 above 15 %), latched motor trips (casing below 85 °C, relay healthy) and LSHH-150 (D-150 below 90 %). Emergency shutdown stops both pumps and closes V100 and TV-110. The Rev C upgrades (MOC after the lazy-twin investigation) add casing pressure transmitters with a high alarm on the idle pump, and motor-operated discharge valves that close when their pump stops.

9 · Field

  • Motors P-200A and P-200B; valves V200, V202, V201, V206, V205 (hand-wheel), casing vents, the header drain.
  • Pump checks: Read PI-210 / PI-220 / PI-209 records a reading (with time) in the log and places the pump on the curve; the text describes noise, vibration, casing temperature, shaft rotation and what the vent shows.
  • Telephones: the tank farm sets HIC-199 (transfer into T200); the cat cracker starts or stops drawing charge (10-minute ramp) and tells you what it sees (answer in 2 minutes).

10 · Exercises

Load an exercise: the plant resets to its starting state and faults appear on their own schedule. The procedure tracker ticks steps when the simulator sees them done (! = out of order). Tick Communicated and press Finish and grade (it also grades itself at the time limit). What-if, trend matching, scrambles and the reading sheet are graded to the Debrief tab.

11 · Debrief and data export

Score with each deduction, performance, exercise grades, fault recovery times and the event log. Export run data, a station snapshot or the event log as UTF-8 CSV. Nothing is kept after the page is closed.

Design of the unit operation · parallel centrifugal pumps P-200A/B

Teaching slide deck · Design of the unit operation — the energy balance from T200 to D-150, pump and system curves, parallel pumps, affinity laws, NPSH, minimum flow, the operating conditions and the conceptual sizing of the station.
Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

How a feed-pump station like this one is specified and roughed out before detailed design. Every number is taken from the simulator's design point (pump A running, FRC-100 at 14 L/s, B the spare) or from offline copies of the model run for this tab; nothing here touches the live simulation. Rules of thumb are quoted as typical practice (API 610, Hydraulic Institute), not as a vendor rating.

1 Fundamentals and principle · 2 Components · 3 Setting the operating conditions · 4 Conceptual design · 5 Conceptual sizing (calculator)

1 · Fundamentals and principle of the unit operation

A pump station moves liquid from a place of low energy (T200, open to the atmosphere, a few metres above the pumps) to a place of higher energy (D-150, at 1.5 bar g and higher up), against friction in pipes, fittings, a strainer, a meter, a heat exchanger and a control valve. A centrifugal pump adds that energy as head — metres of the liquid being pumped. The pump decides how much head it can give at each flow; the piping system decides how much head it needs at each flow. The plant runs where the two curves cross.

2 · Components of the unit operation

The station is two identical horizontal end-suction centrifugal pumps, each in its own leg between a common suction header and a common discharge header. The first sketch is a section through one pump; the second places the pumps in the station. Numbers match the table.

Section through P-200A (not to scale): liquid enters the impeller eye along the shaft axis, is flung outward by the vanes and collected by the volute, which turns velocity into pressure and leads it to the discharge nozzle on top.

3 · Setting the operating conditions (การกำหนดสภาวะในการทำงาน)

For a given cat-cracker demand the station has few independent handles: which pump runs, the FRC-100 set point (moving V100), the steam valve TV-110, and the tank-farm transfer HIC-199 that holds the T200 level. Every other condition — heads, currents, NPSH, casing temperature — follows from these and from the equipment. Each is chosen from a process need and checked against an equipment limit; alarm and trip values below are read from the page's alarm table and the SIS constants.

Order in which the conditions are set

    Operating window

    4 · Conceptual design

    4.1 Design basis

    4.2 Design decisions

    4.3 Design sequence

    1. Duty: normal flow from the consumer (14 L/s), the rated flow with a margin, the liquid (density, viscosity, vapour pressure at the pumping temperature).
    2. Route and ends: suction and delivery pressures and elevations → static head; lowest suction level (the low-low trip level) for the NPSH check.
    3. Line sizes: suction from a low velocity (NPSH), discharge from an economic velocity; check every fitting, the strainer, the meter and the exchanger allowance.
    4. System curve: static + friction (Darcy) + control-valve allowance at the normal and the rated flow.
    5. Number and arrangement of pumps: 1 × 100 %, 2 × 100 % (one spare) or 2 × 50 %; parallel operation needs curves that rise to shut-off and match each other.
    6. Pump selection: rated point near the best-efficiency point, impeller between minimum and maximum diameter, NPSH margin, minimum continuous flow, specific speed.
    7. Power and motor: shaft power at the rated point and at run-out, motor rating with margin, starting, overload setting.
    8. Control valve: opening at minimum, normal and maximum flow; fail position.
    9. Protection: low-level trip of the suction source, deadhead / dry-run protection, motor protection, check valves, high-level protection downstream, ESD.
    10. Data sheet to the vendor (API 610 data sheet) for the hydraulic and mechanical rating.

    5 · Conceptual sizing

    Change any input; the table updates at once. Defaults reproduce the OTS design point; the column OTS design (simulator) shows the simulator's own value for comparison. A ✗ means outside the usual guideline — at the defaults those marks are real findings about this station (read the notes under the table). Size for 16 L/s changes only the flow, so you see what the installed pump cannot do; Fit the impeller to the rated point then changes the impeller diameter by the affinity laws.

    Duty, fluid and the two ends
    Lines, legs and equipment
    Pump and control valve
    Motor, minimum flow, energy

    Assumptions and limits of this sizing

    • Line friction by Darcy–Weisbach with the Swamee–Jain friction factor (64/Re below Re 2300); schedule 40 steel inside diameters; commercial steel roughness 0.046 mm; gas oil kinematic viscosity 3 mm²/s at 60 °C (assumed — the simulator has no viscosity). Equivalent lengths, fitting K-values and the strainer, FE-100 and E-100 allowances are assumed so that the defaults reproduce the model's lumped coefficients (suction 0.01786 m/(L/s)², legs 0.00255, process 0.01916). The allowances scale with (Q/14)².
    • The model takes the delivery static as 24 m (D-150 at 1.5 bar g ≈ 17.6 m of gas oil plus about 6 m of elevation); the calculator uses an inlet 6.42 m above the pumps so that the sum is 24.0 m.
    • The control-valve allowance is entered as a share of the pump head (the teaching deck uses the same definition, 13 %); the V100 openings use the modified equal-percentage characteristic of the simulator, f(x) = (Rx − 1)/(R − 1), and its wide-open loss (1.37 m at 14 L/s).
    • Pump curve H = H0s² − kQ² (the simulator's form); efficiency is an input and is assumed constant between the design and the rated flow. NPSHr = s²[N0 + (NBEP − N0)(Q/QBEP)²] as in the model. Two pumps in parallel are taken as identical.
    • Motor current from the model's line I = 5.5 + 1.35 P and full-load current of the installed 10 kW motor; a different motor size would have its own figures. Motor sizes from the same list as the deck.
    • Deadhead heating uses the model's casing balance (Mc, a loss to air of 0.01 kW/K, start at 60 °C); the alarm and trip temperatures are read from the page.
    • Guidelines quoted (velocities, preferred operating region, head rise, NPSH margin, valve openings, motor margin) are typical design practice (API 610, Hydraulic Institute 9.6.1 / 9.6.3) and are no substitute for a vendor's hydraulic rating. Energy price from the page (training price); running hours assumed.

    3 · Blocks: what goes in, what comes out, what each does

    4 · Streams, design and now

    Read from the Process tab's pcStreams(). Head is metres of liquid above the pump centreline (1 m ≈ 8.5 kPa for this oil). A red Now flow is more than 1 % (or 0.05 L/s for a stream that is zero at design) away from design.

    5 · Balances across the block boundaries

    A BFD is where balances are checked first: draw a boundary round one block (or several) and compare what crosses it. At steady state in = out; during an upset the difference is the accumulation. Each row is computed from the model's own states with the Process tab's balance functions (pcPumpBal, pcTank, pcDrum, pcHeat, pcPower); row 5 is the same E-100 duty computed only from the DCS measurements, the way an engineer would check it. Gap = (in − out) / in. A row turns red only when its gap moves more than 2 points away from its gap at design.

    Balances the DCS cannot close

    • Pumps and header. The DCS measures one flow on the delivery side, FT-100. There is no flow meter on either pump leg, on the suction line or on the header drain. "Made by the pump" can only be inferred: from the local gauges PI-209 and PI-210 / PI-220 against the pump's test curve (they are read in the field, not on the DCS), or roughly from the motor current. So the DCS can never show directly that what a pump makes equals what reaches FE-100; the Process tab (part 7) and the Pump curves tab show how the field readings close that balance.
    • T200. FI-199 (in) and LI-200 are on the DCS, but nothing measures the suction line: the DCS can only compare FI-199 with FT-100 and with the level trend (0.32 % per hour for each 1 L/s of imbalance), so a small difference takes hours to show.
    • D-150. FT-100 (in), FI-151 (out) and LI-150 close this one on the DCS: (FT-100 − FI-151) should equal the level rate times 0.3 m³ per %.
    • E-100. Closes on the DCS (row 5): FI-112, PI-111 (shell pressure → saturation temperature → latent heat), FT-100 and TI-110, with the tank temperature taken as its design 60 °C (T200 has no temperature on the DCS). A growing gap between the two sides means a meter or thermometer is drifting, or the condensate is leaving sub-cooled or with live steam — the model has no such terms, so on the simulator the two sides agree except while TI-110 is moving.
    • Pump energy. Shaft power can be estimated from the motor current (II-210 / II-220); the hydraulic power needs the head across the pump, which only the local gauges give. The model's gap is the pump's own losses (about one third at design), which heat the liquid passing through.

    6 · From BFD to PFD

    • Each block opens into its equipment: "V200 · S-200" becomes a gate valve and a basket strainer on one line; "P-200A" becomes the pump with its own suction valve V202, check valve NRV-210 and discharge valve V201; "FE-100 · V100" becomes an orifice and a fail-closed globe control valve; "E-100" becomes a shell-and-tube exchanger with the steam valve TV-110 and a condensate trap.
    • Each stream gets a flag with flow, temperature and pressure (head) from the heat and mass balance; the PFD numbers its own streams, so the PFD tab shows the matching BFD number beside each flag.
    • The control valves that set the process are added (V100 for the feed, TV-110 for the steam), because they decide where the degrees of freedom are (Control loop design tab, part 4). The hand valve at the tank farm (HIC-199) stays outside.
    • Utilities are drawn where they are used (steam and condensate at E-100, the OWS at the drain); the spare pump is drawn in full, because two pumps in parallel is a design decision, not a detail.
    • Next: the PFD tab, then the P&ID, where the local gauges, the check valves, vents and the trips appear.

    PFD · Process flow diagram PPS-PFD-100

    The pump station drawn as a process engineer issues it: ISO 10628 symbols, Turton stream numbers and information flags, an equipment strip, notes and a title block. Flags carry numbers only where the simulator gives them, and this page sets each one beside the model, at design and now.

    1 What a PFD adds · 2 The drawing · 3 Equipment list · 4 Flags and the model · 5 Reading the PFD · 6 What the P&ID adds · 7 Teaching notes

    1 · What a PFD adds to the BFD

    • Equipment instead of blocks: the tank, the strainer, both pumps in their parallel legs, the preheater and the drum, each with its tag and a symbol in proportion to the real item (T200 Ø 12 m × 10 m dominates; D-150 is 30 m³).
    • Its own stream numbers (1–10, left to right, Turton style). They are not the Process-tab numbers: the PFD splits the suction into the strainer outlet and the two pump legs, and labels steam and condensate as utilities instead of numbering them. Section 4 gives the matching Process/BFD number in brackets.
    • Information flags (liquid flow in L/s, temperature in °C, pressure in bar g, steam in t/h) on the streams the model can give, from the design state.
    • The control valves that define the process: the tank-farm transfer (HIC-199), the feed (V100 by FRC-100) and the steam (TV-110 by TIC-110). These are the handles an operator has; everything else on the line is open or shut.
    • The spare is drawn. On many PFDs a spared pump is one symbol tagged A/B; here the two legs are drawn apart because the parallel arrangement is the subject of this simulator.

    5 · Reading the PFD

      6 · What the P&ID adds

      • Every valve: the common suction valve V200 at the tank, the suction block valves V202/V206, the discharge block valves V201/V205, the casing vents VA/VB and the header low-point drain — the valves that make a line-up, and the ones a field operator can get wrong.
      • The check valves NRV-210 and NRV-220, one on each pump discharge between the pump and its block valve. They are the only thing that stops header liquid running backwards through the idle leg, and a PFD cannot show them.
      • Local instruments that never reach the DCS: PI-209 on the suction header and PI-210/PI-220 on each casing (between the pump and its check valve).
      • Protection: LSLL-200 (both pumps), TSHH-212/222 (casing temperature), the 49-210/220 motor overloads, LSHH-150 (forces V100 closed), the ESD and their final elements; fail positions (V100 and TV-110 fail closed).
      • Line sizes, specifications and line numbers, the FE-100 orifice run, steam trap and condensate return details.
      • See the P&ID tab: the EPC sheet PPS-PID-001 and the screen drawing used by the DCS.

        Operating windows · where the pump station can run, what limits it, and how much room there is

        Teaching slide deck — operability of the feed pump station: variability, bounds and the integrity operating window, capacity and turndown of one and two pumps, and the Type I, II and III windows worked on this model.
        Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

        Follows the course lecture Operating Windows (after T. Marlin's Process Operability class materials). Every window on this tab was computed on copies of this simulator's own model, each run to steady state with the trips switched off (so a limit is seen rather than cut short) and the tank and drum levels held. The live plant is never touched. Limits come from the page's alarms (ALM), the trip settings (K) and the valve ranges; limits marked "assumed" are teaching values.

        1 Operability · 2 Variability · 3 Bounds and IOW · 4 Worst case and point check · 5 Capacity and turndown · 6 Type I window · 7 Type II and III window · 8 Monte Carlo window · 9 Manipulated variables · 10 Holes and limitations

        1 · Operability and the operating window

        Process operability means the plant has the capacity and flexibility to reach a range of operating conditions safely, reliably, profitably, with good dynamic performance and product quality. The operating window is the range of achievable steady-state operation: the set of conditions for which every controlled variable can be held at its set point and no limit is broken. It is shaped by four things.

        The variables of the pump station

        ClassVariable (tag)DesignWhy it is in this class

        The station is a flow-delivery unit: its product is a flow at a pressure and a temperature. Its one controlled rate is FRC-100, whose set point the cat cracker writes. The window question is therefore: which feed rates can the cat cracker ask for, with which pumps, at which tank level and with which suction and steam conditions, without breaking a limit?

        2 · Variability: the design basis the window must cover

        "The abnormal is normal." A window is only as good as the list of changes it was sized for. The lecture's five sources of variability, written as a design-basis memorandum for the station (ranges are the ones swept on this tab; frequencies are teaching values):

        SourceWhat changes at the stationRange used hereHow oftenCovered by

        A single human error must not cause an unsafe condition and must not stay undetected. That is why the fast bounds of part 3 carry alarms and, where damage is quick (dry running, a deadheaded pump, an overloaded motor, an overfilled drum), trips.

        3 · Bounds and the integrity operating window

        The bounds are the frame of the window. A capacity bound is a handle at the end of its travel; a physical bound is a law of nature (a pump cavitates when the suction pressure approaches the vapour pressure); a hard bound must not be crossed (trip settings, the motor rating, the pump's minimum flow); a soft bound can be crossed for a while (alarms); the quality bound is the cat cracker's feed-temperature band; the CV bound is the control objective itself. When a point fails, the page lists the violated bounds in this order, so the root cause comes first: a pump starved of suction pressure (cavitation) explains a valve at 100 %, and a valve at 100 % explains a flow below set point, not the other way round. When V100 is wide open while the NPSH margin is below 0.5 m, the pump is being held at its cavitation edge and the maps call the point suction-limited.

        IdBoundSourceKindScale for the margin

        Live margins: the plant now against the design point

        Margin now ÷ margin at design. Values are what the DCS shows: FT-100, the controller outputs (not the field valve positions), the motor currents and casing temperatures, the levels. Pump flow and NPSH are not measured at this station; their rows are estimates from FT-100 and LI-200 assuming equal sharing, a clean strainer and design vapour pressure, and say so. Updated live.

        BoundKindLimitDesignNowMargin now ÷ design

        Reading the ladder (API RP 584 integrity operating windows). Inside the target range the pumps and the preheater run reliably. Between the target and the standard limit (the alarm) the station is still safe, but time counts: seal wear, bearing heat, cavitation erosion or off-spec feed accumulate. Past the critical limit (the trip, or the physical edge) damage is quick; that is where the motor protection and the SIS act. The arrow is the live value.

        4 · Design for the worst case, and a live point check

        Equipment is sized for the worst case of the variability it must handle. For a centrifugal pump the hydraulic worst case is the highest flow with the lowest suction pressure (lowest tank level, dirtiest strainer, most volatile feed); for the preheater it is the highest flow with the lowest steam pressure; for the pump's minimum flow it is the lowest rate, worst with two pumps sharing it. Pick a case, or set your own point: the page runs this model to steady state on a copy (FRC-100 in AUTO at the set point, trips off, levels held) and checks every bound.

        5 · Capacity and turndown

        A station that only just meets the design point is cheap but has no window; a large one has a window but costs capital and wastes energy throttling at normal rate. The lecture's rule: capacity must keep the plant safe, protect expensive equipment and meet quality for the base case and the frequently occurring variability; a lower rate is acceptable in rare cases; stop for the extreme ones. Turndown ratio = normal maximum ÷ normal minimum, where "normal" means sustainable without hazard or damage.

        5a · Maximum flow: V100 wide open (FRC-100 in MAN at 100 %)

        5b · The station as a series plant

        Each element allows its own range of feed. The station's range is the overlap of all of them, so it is always smaller than any single element's. Ranges below are read along the Type III grid of part 7 at the chosen tank level, interpolated between the 1 L/s grid points. ◀ / ▶ = the element still allows more at the end of the swept range (2–22 L/s). A bound is shown as met where the flow never reaches it (for example TI-110 at a demand one pump cannot deliver): the element that stops the flow first is the one that matters.

        ElementTurndown or rangeability at this stationTypical (lecture)Flexibility class

        7 · Type II and Type III: the disturbances the station can absorb

        Now FRC-100 holds the feed at the set point the cat cracker asks for while the tank level and the other disturbances move. Type II reads the handle positions each point needs; Type III keeps only the points where every handle is inside its range and every bound holds, and colours the rest by the bound that fails first (root cause first).

        8 · Monte Carlo operating window

        The lecture's recipe: (1) simulate the base case, (2) replace the uncertain inputs by samples from their distributions and repeat, (3) mark each sample feasible or infeasible against every bound, (4) report the fraction and show it graphically. Here the cat-cracker demand is normal, the tank level uniform between two values and the strainer fouling uniform from clean to a maximum; each sample's margin is interpolated in the Type III grids of part 7 (strainer between the clean, 25 % and 50 % planes).

        9 · Manipulated variables: enough, strong, independent, fast

        With n adjustable handles and m variables to hold: n = m gives a finite window with each point exactly specified; n < m gives no window (at best the design point) and is not an acceptable design; n > m leaves extra freedom (several ways to reach a point, which can be used to optimise).

        Held variable (m)Handle (n)Steady-state effect of the handle (open loop, from the design point)
        Lecture criterionCheck at this station

        10 · Holes in the window, and what the steady-state window does not tell you

        • Only steady states. A set-point step, a pump start or a steam disturbance leaves the window for a while even when the end point is inside it. The Control loop design and Transition operation tabs deal with the dynamics.
        • Levels are held. T200 and D-150 are inventories: at steady state the tank-farm transfer must equal the feed and the feed must equal the cat cracker's draw, or a level runs away. The window is computed at fixed levels; part 9 shows the level rates that a mismatch produces.
        • Large excursions are outside the method: priming, start-up, change-over, trips and restart have their own procedures and limits (SIS tab, procedures).
        • Model structure is assumed right. Pump wear, impeller damage, valve trim wear and meter errors change A, B and C; the window shrinks. Re-run a point with the conditions you expect.
        • Unmeasured bounds. Pump flow and NPSH are not measured at this station, so two of the bounds that set the edges of the window cannot be watched directly by the operator (Flexibility tab, recommendations).
        • Curse of dimensionality. Feed × level at 21 × 9 points, six cases and three pump choices already took several thousand runs; every added variable multiplies that.

        References: T. Marlin, Process Operability class materials (2013); course lecture Operating Windows; API RP 584 Integrity Operating Windows; ANSI/HI 9.6.1 Rotodynamic Pumps — Guideline for NPSH Margin; ANSI/HI 9.6.3 Allowable Operating Region; API 610 Centrifugal Pumps.

        Follows the course lecture Flexibility (after T. Marlin's Process Operability class materials). The Operating windows tab finds where the station can run; this tab looks at the handles that move it there. Gains and capacities come from runs on copies of this simulator's model (embedded with the Operating windows tab); the pump, system and valve curves are the model's own healthy-equipment hydraulics (the same calculation as the Pump curves tab), and the E-100 calculator solves the model's own preheater equations at steady state. The live plant is never touched.

        1 What flexibility is · 2 How many · 3 Where · 4 Fluid flow · 5 Heat transfer · 6 Production rate · 7 How much · 8 Throttle or slow the pump · 9 Recommendations

        1 · What flexibility is

        Flexibility is the ability of a plant to operate reliably across a wide range of rates and conditions without losing quantity or quality. Some controlled variables are held at their set points while disturbances arrive; flexibility is what lets us steer the process after the equipment has been built.

        Without flexibility the process does not respond to set-point changes and passes every disturbance on to rate, quality and safety. With flexibility it reaches its set points and compensates the disturbances.

        How it is provided

        • Spare capacity in pumps, valves, exchangers, vessels, motor speed — and installed spare equipment.
        • Adjustable utility flows: steam, cooling water, fuel, air.
        • By-passes that send part of a flow around equipment.
        • Inventory that absorbs a mismatch for a while.

        Four design questions: how many handles, where, which tools (valves, speed, by-passes), and how much capacity.

        The flexibility register of the pump station

        HandleWhat it adjustsKind of flexibilityAt designSpare at designStatus

        2 · How many handles? Degrees of freedom

        A successful design needs number of adjustable handles ≥ number of variables to be held. The maximum number of controlled variables equals the degrees of freedom, and the minimum number of handles equals the number of variables we insist on.

        Variable the station must holdWhyHandle usedWho moves it

        3 · Where? Causal paths from each handle

        Each held variable needs a handle with an independent causal path to it. Interaction is allowed as long as every desired point can still be reached. The lecture's three cases, found at this station:

        Steady-state effect of each handle from the design point, all loops in manual, run on the model (the numbers behind the causal map). Shaded cells are the large effects.

        Interaction one way: V100 and TV-110 on feed flow and TI-110

        V100 moves the flow and, through the flow, TI-110; TV-110 moves only TI-110. Ask for a change and the page solves the 2 × 2 steady-state model (gains from the +5 % runs above) for the two valve moves:

        A two-way pair, if a speed drive were added: V100 and pump speed on flow and header pressure

        4 · Flexibility for fluid flow

        For a liquid the flow settles where the pump's head equals the head the system needs: Hpump(Q, n) = ΔHstatic + (Kline + Kvalve(x)) Q². Only two terms can be adjusted: the valve resistance Kvalve(x) (throttling) or the pump curve itself (speed n, or the number of pumps running).

        4a · Pump, system and valve curves

        Healthy curves from the model: pump ΔH = H0(n/3600)² − k·Q² (affinity laws: shut-off head ∝ n²), k = m/(L/s)²; system = delivery static head minus the tank head, plus the suction line and strainer, the leg valves, FE-100, E-100 and line, and V100 (modified equal percentage, R = 30). The operating point is solved by the same network routine as the Pump curves tab, T200 at its design level.

        4b · Two pumps in parallel: why the flow does not double

        4c · The installed characteristic of V100, from the model's own Kproc(x)

        5 · Flexibility for heat transfer: the steam preheater E-100

        Q = U A ΔT*: flexibility can act on U (a flow changes a film coefficient), on A (the condensing area, for example by flooding part of the shell with condensate), or on ΔT (a utility's pressure or flow, or a by-pass that mixes).

        Term at E-100What sets itHandle today

        The lecture's three cases, applied to E-100 (goal: hold TI-110)

        CaseFeed (cold side)Steam (hot side)FlexibilityAt this station
        afixed by production (FRC-100)adjustableadjust the steam: TV-110 sets the shell pressure, and so the condensing temperatureAs built: TV-110, TIC-110 normally in MAN. Fast enough, but the operator closes the loop.
        bfixed by productionfixed (header pressure, valve wide open)by-pass part of the feed around E-100 and mixNot installed. Fast (mixing), but the tubes then see less flow and run hotter (watch fouling of a heavy feed).
        cfixed by productionfixed supplyvary the condensing area: a condensate-level valve floods part of the tubesNot installed. Smooth and cheap in steam traps, but slow (level dynamics).

        Model relations (steady state of step()): steam W = Cs·x·√(Psup² − Psh²); tube side Tout = Tin + (Tsat(Psh) − Tin)(1 − e−UA/C); W·λ = C (Tout − Tin). The by-pass case is the lecture's case b added to the same equations (the simulator itself has no by-pass); the by-passed feed rejoins at T200 temperature.

        6 · Flexibility for production rate

        At steady state material must balance in every unit and in the whole plant (no long-term accumulation). One flexible variable sets the rate; every other flow should follow automatically without people, and measured flows are never simply matched to each other (meter errors would accumulate). Levels show the inventories.

        Guiding principleAt this station

        7 · How much capacity? Spare room on each handle

        Move the demand, the tank level and the pump choice: the bars show how far each handle must go to hold the point (Type II runs of the Operating windows tab, interpolated; V100 from the as-operated case, TV-110 from the TIC-110 AUTO case). The first bar to reach 95 % is the capacity that sets the top of the window.

        8 · Throttle the flow, or slow the pump?

        A throttling valve buys flexibility by burning head: the pump makes more head than the system needs and V100 takes the difference. A variable-speed drive (VSD) moves the pump curve instead, so the valve can stay nearly open. The lecture's question: which tool gives the flexibility, at what cost?

        HAZID · Hazard identification of the parallel pump station

        A plant-level, checklist-driven identification of what could go badly wrong around the cat-cracker feed pumps — the tank, the suction, the pump bay, the discharge and its control valve, the steam preheater, the feed drum, the utilities and the site — done before (and wider than) the detailed HAZOP. It uses the same example risk matrix as the HAZOP tab; a real study uses the owner's matrix, a multidisciplinary team and the plot plan.

        Teaching slide deck · HAZID — what HAZID is, PPS-PFD-100 and its study areas, the guideword checklist, bow-tie thinking, the register and the major accident hazards of a hot-oil pump station.
        Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

        1 What HAZID is · 2 Method · 3 PFD and study areas · 4 Guideword checklist · 5 Hazard register · 6 Major accident hazards · 7 From HAZID to HAZOP · Teaching notes

        1 · What HAZID is and where it sits

        HAZID (hazard identification) is a structured brainstorm of what could go badly wrong across the whole facility, including its surroundings, its people and the environment. It is done early — concept and front-end design — on the PFD, the layout and the design basis, so that the major hazards shape the design (spacing, bunds, isolation, trips) before the details are fixed. It asks broad questions ("what hazards does a bay of hot-oil pumps bring?"); HAZOP asks detailed ones ("what if there is no flow out of P-200A while it runs?").

        HAZIDHAZOP
        WhenConcept / FEED, and before a major changeDetailed design with the P&ID frozen; revalidation every few years
        DrawingPFD (here PPS-PFD-100), plot planP&ID (PPS-PID-001), cause-and-effect chart
        BreakdownAreas / systemsNodes with one design intent (e.g. "P-200A delivers 14 L/s into the header")
        PromptGuideword checklist by hazard category (natural, external, process, rotating equipment, utilities, ignition, health, occupational, environment, operations, people)Guide word × parameter (NO flow, REVERSE flow, MORE temperature, LESS level …)
        ScopeProcess and non-process hazards, site and surroundingsProcess deviations and operability
        OutputHazard register, list of major accident hazards (MAH), studies to do next (HAZOP, fire and explosion, SIL, layout, occupational exposure)Worksheets and recommendations per deviation
        ReferenceISO 17776 (major accident hazard management in design; HAZID and its checklist); company HSE practiceIEC 61882

        2 · Method

        1. Define scope and basis: from the tank-farm transfer into T200 to the cat-cracker charge pump on D-150, with the steam supply, power and instrument air; the fluid (gas oil, 870 kg/m³, stored at 60 °C, heated to about 150 °C); site conditions; the risk matrix.
        2. Divide the plant into areas on the PFD (section 3).
        3. Apply the guideword checklist to each area (section 4): for each category ask whether the hazard exists here, what could release it (cause / threat) and what would follow (top event and outcome).
        4. Record the existing controls, split into prevention (stops the top event) and mitigation (limits the outcome), as in a bow-tie.
        5. Rank the risk (S × L with the controls) and flag major accident hazards (MAH): events that could cause a fatality, a major fire or a major release.
        6. Assign actions and further studies: design changes, HAZOP nodes, fire and explosion analysis, SIL assessment, layout review, maintenance and isolation standards.
        What makes a pump station different: the fluid is not very volatile but it is hot and plentiful — hundreds of cubic metres in one tank, and the feed leaves E-100 well above its flash point. The machines bring their own failure modes (cavitation, running dead-headed, reverse rotation) and the spare brings two more: an idle leg that can pass liquid backwards, and a machine that is maintained while its twin runs beside it. Flash point {A:flash} °C and autoignition temperature {A:ait} °C are assumed values for this teaching example.

        6 · Major accident hazards and what they lead to

          7 · From HAZID to HAZOP and other studies

          • Every process hazard is examined in detail in the HAZOP tab, node by node on the P&ID (table below): the HAZID says that a dead-head or a reverse flow matters; the HAZOP asks what causes it on this P&ID, what the operator sees and whether the safeguards are enough.
          • The trips that protect against the MAH and their precursors — LSHH-150 → V100 (D-150 overfill), LSLL-200 (pumps losing suction), TSHH-212/222 (dead-head) — go to the Safety layers and LOPA tabs and a SIL assessment (IEC 61511); the SRS of SIF and C&E matrix tabs specify them.
          • The fire hazards (HD-01, HD-03, HD-07, HD-15, HD-16, HD-23, HD-28) go to a fire and explosion analysis, hazardous-area classification and a layout / separation check of the tank, the pump bay and the drum.
          • Maintenance and occupational hazards (HD-06, HD-11, HD-12, HD-13, HD-19) go to the permit-to-work and isolation standards and the occupational-exposure programme.
          • The register is revisited under management of change: a new feed (lighter, sour), a third pump, a new control scheme or auto-start of the spare.

            Read in order: what must be controlled and why, the vocabulary of a loop, the variables of the station, its degrees of freedom, the loops on the P&ID, why those loops were chosen, the loop structures, and finally P, PI and PID with step tests and a tuning lab.             1 Control objectives · 2 The feedback loop · 3 Variables · 4 Degrees of freedom · 5 Loops on the P&ID · 6 How the loops were chosen · 7 Loop structures · 8 P, PI and PID · 9 Tuning lab

            1 · Control objectives (ต้องการควบคุมอะไร และเพราะอะไร)

            Control design starts from objectives, not from instruments. They are ranked: a lower objective is never met by giving up a higher one — the cat cracker's rate is never kept up by running a pump that is cavitating, deadheaded or overloaded, and the feed temperature is never held by letting the drum overfill.

            2 · The feedback loop: parts and vocabulary

            In this simulator OUT is always shown as % open of the valve. Both control valves here fail closed (air to open), so the signal and the opening move together; with a fail-open valve the signal to the actuator would be inverted in the field (at the positioner), and the operator would still see % open. The action is chosen from the process (more opening → more flow, more steam → hotter), the fail position from the safe state; the two are independent.

            4 · Degrees of freedom (DOF)

            Why it matters. The degrees of freedom tell the designer how many variables can be held independently. Control more CVs than there are independent MVs and controllers fight over one valve; control fewer and some variable drifts wherever the disturbances push it — which is exactly what the two tank levels do here, on purpose.

            NDOF = Nvariables − Nindependent equations  =  Ndisturbances (fixed by the surroundings) + Nmanipulated

            4.1 Variables and equations of the station (pump A running, B idle with its check valve holding, drain shut)

            4.2 How each DOF is used

            DOF (handle)Used to fixByWhy
            V100Feed flow QpFRC-100 (auto; set point from the cat cracker)Direct, fast and one-signed (section 6). The feed rate is the cat cracker's decision, so its set point comes from there.
            TV-110E-100 outlet ToutTIC-110 — normally manual (fixed opening), auto availableA fixed opening gives a fixed steam supply; the outlet then moves with the feed rate (section 7 shows by how much). In AUTO the same handle holds Tout.
            HIC-199T200 inventory (dV200/dt = 0 on average)Tank-farm operator (manual, by phone)The transfer pump belongs to the tank farm; the tank is so large that a hand setting holds it for many hours.
            Cat-cracker charge (Qfcc)D-150 inventoryThe cat cracker (it is a DV for this station)The feed rate and the charge rate are both the cat cracker's; it matches them and watches LI-150.
            Pump selection, line-up (discrete)Which equations exist (one leg or two, idle legs isolated or not)Operator and proceduresDiscrete handles do not add a continuous DOF; they change the network the continuous ones act on (a second pump changes the pump-curve equation, an open idle leg adds one).

            4.3 DOF of each loop, and the two levels that are not on automatic

            • A feedback loop uses one DOF: it turns "valve position is free" into "CV = SP". The SP becomes the new free input, given by the operator, a master controller or — here — the cat cracker.
            • Cascade, ratio and feedforward do not create DOF; they act through the same valve. A controller in MAN gives its DOF back to the operator (TIC-110 normally). A saturated valve loses its DOF: FRC-100 at 100 % output no longer holds the flow — the pumps set it.
            • Two controllers never move one valve without a selector or a split range. On this unit the SIS overrides FRC-100 when LSHH-150 or the ESD acts: the controller is forced to track 0 % and its DOF is taken away until reset.

            5 · The control loops on the P&ID

            Blue: feed; red: steam; teal: condensate. Dashed black: control signals; dashed red: SIS and motor protection; dashed orange: Rev C additions and possible upgrades (section 7). Bubbles with a single line are on the DCS, without a line are local gauges. The table reads the tuning, set points and modes of the running session live.

            6 · How the loops were chosen for this P&ID (หลักการกำหนด control loop ตาม P&ID)

            1. Start from the objectives and the DOF. Three continuous handles (V100, TV-110, HIC-199), so at most three variables can be held. The feed rate is the station's job; the temperature is a quality wish; the T200 level is the tank farm's.
            2. Pair each CV with the MV that affects it most directly, fast and with one sign. The step tests below give the numbers: V100 moves the flow within seconds and does not move the temperature much; TV-110 moves only the temperature, and slowly. The pairing FRC-100 → V100, TIC-110 → TV-110 is the only sensible one.
            3. Fast flow loop on the valve. FRC-100 removes pump-side disturbances (suction loss, tank level, a second pump, wear) within seconds, as long as V100 has room left.
            4. Know where the gain lives. V100's effect on the flow changes a lot along its stroke (table below): a tuning that is right at 84 % open is several times more aggressive at 50 %.
            5. Throttle, or change the speed? With a large static head a speed drive saves little power here (table below), and the fail-closed V100 is also a shut-off the SIS uses; throttling is the design choice.
            6. Keep safety separate from control. The pump protection reads its own switches and relays, not FT-100 or TE-110.
            7. Choose fail positions for the safe state: V100 fails closed (no uncontrolled feed into D-150, which can overfill), TV-110 fails closed (no steam on oil that may have stopped moving).
            8. Slow, rarely changed handles stay in manual with alarms: TV-110 (the feed rate changes seldom), HIC-199 (a huge tank), the D-150 level (the cat cracker's own balance).
            9. No automatic start of the spare on this revision (below).

            7 · Loop structures: the principle of each (หลักการพื้นฐานของ control loop แต่ละแบบ)

            StructurePrincipleUse it whenOn this station
            Manual (open loop)The operator sets the valve; nothing corrects disturbances.The variable changes rarely, or automatic action would cost more than it saves.Used: TIC-110 normally (TV-110 at a fixed opening), HIC-199 at the tank farm
            Single feedbackMeasure the CV, compare with SP, move the MV until the error is gone. Corrects any disturbance, but only after it has moved the CV.Almost always the base layer.Used: FRC-100 → V100; TIC-110 → TV-110 when in AUTO
            Remote set pointAnother unit (or a master controller) writes the SP.The rate belongs to a downstream unit.Used: the cat cracker sets the FRC-100 set point
            CascadeThe master sets the SP of a faster slave, which removes its own disturbances before they reach the master's CV. Slave 3–5 × faster (or more).A fast disturbance acts between the valve and the CV.Upgrade: TIC-110 → FIC-112 (steam flow, FI-112 is already on the DCS) → TV-110: a steam-header pressure drop is corrected by the steam-flow loop in seconds instead of by TIC-110 over minutes
            RatioOne flow's SP = ratio × another (wild) flow.A utility must follow a process flow.Upgrade: steam SP = (steam/feed ratio) × FT-100; the ratio needed for 150 °C is nearly constant (table below)
            FeedforwardMeasure a disturbance and move the MV before the CV changes, using a model; it needs feedback trim because the model is never exact.A large, measurable disturbance.Upgrade: FT-100 → TV-110 bias, trimmed by TIC-110 (study below)
            Averaging level controlA loose level loop lets the level swing inside its alarms so that the outflow changes slowly.A buffer tank between two units.Possible: LIC-150 → FRC-100 set point (the feed would follow the charge); not used, because the cat cracker wants to set its feed itself
            Override / selectorA selector passes the lower (or higher) of two signals so a constraint takes over when it is reached.Protect a constraint while normally controlling another CV.Used, as a forced override: LSHH-150 and ESD force V100 closed. Upgrade: a minimum-flow recycle (FIC with a valve back to T200) that opens when the pump flow falls, so a forced-closed V100 no longer deadheads the running pump
            Split rangeOne controller output drives two valves in sequence (0–50 % valve A, 50–100 % valve B).One CV needs two handles (heat and cool, small and large valve).Not used: one steam valve covers the range. It would appear if a small and a large TV were fitted in parallel for turndown
            SIS interlocks and motor protectionDiscrete logic on independent sensors drives the plant to a safe state; latched until reset.Hazards that control cannot be trusted with.Used: LSLL-200 (both pumps), TSHH-212/222 and 49-210/220 (own motor), LSHH-150 (V100 closed), ESD; start permissives (SIS reset, LSL-200, no motor trip latched, suction open, casing primed)

            Feedforward from the feed flow to the steam: a study on the model

            8 · Control modes: P, PI and PID (แนวทางการควบคุม P, PI, PID)

            The simulator's controller (pid() in the model) uses the ideal PID form with signals in % of the transmitter span (FRC-100 0–20 L/s, TIC-110 0–250 °C), derivative on the measurement (filtered with Td/8), bumpless transfer and an anti-windup clamp:

            e = SP% − PV% (reverse) or PV% − SP% (direct),   OUT = Kc e + I + D,   dI/dt = Kc e / Ti,   D = ∓Kc Td dPV%/dt

            • Bumpless: when a loop goes to AUTO the integral starts at I = OUT − Kce − D, so OUT does not jump.
            • Anti-windup: if OUT would pass 0 or 100 %, it is clamped and the integral is reset so that OUT sits exactly on the limit; it leaves the limit as soon as the error changes sign. FRC-100 at 100 % with a short flow therefore does not wind up.
            • P only (Ti = 0): the integral stays at its starting value (the bias), so any load or set-point change leaves an offset.
            • Tracking: while LSHH-150 or the ESD forces V100 closed, FRC-100 tracks (OUT = 0, integral re-initialised), so the return to control after the reset is bumpless.

            8.1 What each term does

            ModeActionGoodBadTypical use
            P (proportional)OUT change ∝ error now.Simple, immediate.Offset after a load change: e = Δload / (1 + KcK). With the small process gains here (well below 1 %/%) the offset is almost the whole change unless Kc is large. High gain → oscillation.Averaging level control.
            PI (+ integral)Adds the accumulated error; keeps moving OUT until the error is zero.No offset for steps. The industrial default.Overshoot if Ti is short; windup at a saturated valve (prevented here).Flow, pressure, most temperature and level loops.
            PID (+ derivative)Adds action ∝ rate of change of PV; anticipates.Faster, less overshoot on slow, lag-dominated loops with clean signals.Amplifies noise; derivative on error kicks on SP changes (hence derivative on PV). Useless on a flow loop (noise, almost no lag).Slow temperature loops with several lags.

            8.2 Guidelines by loop type, and the tuning on this station

            8.3 Tuning from a step test (FOPDT model)

            Put the loop in MAN, step OUT, record PV. Fit a first-order-plus-dead-time model G(s) = K e−θs/(τs + 1): K = ΔPV/ΔOUT (both in % of span); from the times to 28.3 % and 63.2 % of the final change, τ = 1.5 (t63 − t28), θ = t63 − τ. Then the lambda (IMC) PI rule with a chosen closed-loop time constant λ: Kc = τ / [K(λ + θ)], Ti = τ. λ = τ gives a smooth loop, λ = τ/3 a tight one.

              1 Standard and method · 2 Team and documents · 3 Nodes · 4 Guide words and parameters · 5 Risk matrix · 6 Worksheets · 7 Coverage check · 8 Recommendations · 9 Dynamic check on the simulator · 10 Follow-up and close-out

              1 · Standard and method (IEC 61882)

              HAZOP is a structured, team-based examination of a defined system. Each part of the design is compared with its design intent; guide words combined with process parameters generate deviations; for each credible deviation the team records causes, consequences, existing safeguards and, where the risk is not acceptable, recommendations. It finds both hazards (harm to people, environment, assets) and operability problems (the station cannot deliver the feed the cat cracker asks for). On a pump station with an installed spare, the hazards sit as much in the idle equipment — a check valve that no longer seats, a casing blocked in for maintenance — as in the running pump, so REVERSE (back-flow through an idle pump, a pump turning backwards) and the procedure node matter as much as NO flow.

              ReferenceWhat it contributes
              IEC 61882:2016 Hazard and operability studies (HAZOP studies) – Application guideDefinitions, the four phases (definition, preparation, examination, documentation and follow-up), guide words, team roles, recording
              CCPS Guidelines for Hazard Evaluation Procedures (3rd ed.)Worksheet format, node selection, procedural HAZOP, "consequence without safeguards", risk ranking, links to LOPA
              IEC 61511 (functional safety, SIS)How HAZOP scenarios feed LOPA and SIL targets for the trips LSLL-200, TSHH-212/222 and LSHH-150 and for proposed ones (low-flow trip, overfill protection)
              API 610 (centrifugal pumps), API 682 (seals), API 2350 (tank overfill), API 2000 (tank venting)Minimum continuous flow, reverse rotation, seal arrangements, overfill and vacuum protection used as the basis for safeguards
              ISO 31000 / owner's risk matrixRisk criteria used to decide whether safeguards are adequate
              Thailand: Department of Industrial Works regulation on hazard identification, risk assessment and risk-management plans (B.E. 2543)Legal requirement to identify hazards (HAZOP is an accepted method) and to prepare risk-management plans for factories
              OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 (PSM), where applicableProcess hazard analysis for covered processes, revalidated at least every five years

              The four phases

              1. Definition: scope from the tank-farm transfer valve (HIC-199) through T200, the suction, P-200A/B with their check and block valves, the discharge header, FE-100/V100, E-100 (steam and feed sides) to the D-150 inlet and the interface with the cat cracker (remote set point, LALL-150); excluded: the tank farm, the steam system upstream of TV-110 and the cat-cracker unit itself. Objectives, team, risk matrix.
              2. Preparation: collect the P&ID, the pump curves, the process and design data, the trip and alarm list, the start-up, change-over and shutdown procedures, datasheets; divide the plant into nodes; write each node's design intent; choose parameters and guide words.
              3. Examination: for each node → state the design intent → choose a parameter → apply each guide word → is the deviation meaningful? → causes → consequences assuming the safeguards fail → existing safeguards → rank the risk → recommend → next guide word. Record every meaningful deviation, including those with adequate safeguards ("full recording"), so the reasoning can be audited.
              4. Documentation and follow-up: worksheets, recommendation register with owners and dates, action close-out, and revalidation after changes (MOC) or periodically.

              2 · Team and documents

              RoleResponsibility
              HAZOP leader (chair)Independent of the design; runs the method, keeps the team on the node, decides when a deviation is covered
              Scribe (recorder)Writes the worksheet live, reads back recommendations
              Process engineer (designer)Design intent, hydraulics (system and pump curves, NPSH), heat balance of E-100
              Operations representativeHow the station is really run: rounds, the spare on standby, change-over, the cat-cracker interface
              Instrument / control engineerLoops, fail positions, trips and permissives, which transmitter each trip reads
              Safety / risk engineerRisk matrix, LOPA follow-up, regulations
              Specialists as neededRotating equipment (pumps, seals, check valves), electrical (motor protection, phase sequence), cat-cracker operations

              Documents for this study: P&ID tab (PPS-V1-PID-001 rev A and its notes), Process tab (stream table, balances), Pump curves tab (curves, NPSH), Design and Control loop design tabs, SIS tab (trips, permissives, Rev C options), Workbook tab (alarm list), the start-up, change-over and shutdown procedures in the Exercises tab.

              3 · Nodes

              A node is a part of the plant with one clear design intent. Boundaries are put where the intent changes: the tank holds, the suction delivers liquid with enough NPSH, each pump raises the head, the header and V100 meter the flow, E-100 heats, D-150 buffers. The two pump legs are separate nodes because their intents differ — one runs, the other must stay ready and must not let liquid back. Procedures get their own node N8 because start-up, change-over and maintenance of the spare create deviations that steady running does not.

              4 · Guide words and parameters

              Parameters used: flow, pressure, temperature, level, composition, rotation, current, integrity (containment), measurement, control, and for procedures: sequence, timing, maintenance, electrical work, restart. A deviation is recorded only if it is physically meaningful ("REVERSE temperature" is not; REVERSE flow and REVERSE rotation are).

              5 · Risk matrix (example for teaching)

              Numbers in brackets: how many deviations of this study fall in the cell. Risk = S × L (the same matrix ranks the HAZID register).

              SSeverity (worst credible consequence, no credit for safeguards)
              1No injury; short feed upset
              2First aid; feed off target or a pump damaged; small contained spill
              3Lost-time injury; cat cracker loses its feed (unit trip); pump out for days; local release
              4Permanent disability or single fatality; gas-oil fire at the pumps or the tank; major equipment damage
              5Multiple fatalities; tank fire spreading beyond the bund; escalation to the cat cracker
              LLikelihood with the existing safeguards
              1Remote: not expected in the life of the plant (< 10⁻⁴ /y)
              2Unlikely: known in industry (10⁻⁴–10⁻³ /y)
              3Possible: could happen in the plant life (10⁻³–10⁻² /y)
              4Likely: several times in the plant life (10⁻²–10⁻¹ /y)
              5Frequent: yearly or more

              1–4 Low acceptable · 5–9 Medium reduce if practicable (ALARP), review safeguards · 10–16 High recommendation required, consider LOPA · 20–25 Very high not acceptable, act before operation

              6 · HAZOP worksheets (node by node)

              Consequences are written assuming the safeguards fail (worst credible case). S ranks that consequence; L ranks its likelihood with the listed safeguards working as designed. Safeguard settings are read from the simulator's own trip and alarm tables; "fault library" marks a cause that the Instructor station can inject.

              7 · Coverage check: guide words applied in each node

              A dot means that guide word gave no meaningful deviation for any parameter in the node (it was still considered). EARLY / LATE / BEFORE / AFTER apply mainly to the procedure node N8.

              8 · Recommendation register

              9 · Dynamic check of selected deviations on the simulator

              A conventional HAZOP judges consequences qualitatively. Here ten deviations are run on copies of the pump-station model from the design state (P-200A running at 14 L/s, B lined up, FRC-100 in AUTO, TIC-110 in MAN) with the existing safeguards active — alarms, SIS and motor-protection trips, controllers in their normal modes, tank and drum levels free to move — and no operator action, for 30 min. The result shows whether the safeguards act before harm and how much time the operator has. Alarms are checked every second with the page's alarm table and its suppression rules; the live simulator is not touched.

              What the runs tell the HAZOP team

                10 · Follow-up and close-out

                • Each recommendation gets an owner and a due date; the owner answers accepted and done, accepted with an alternative (with justification) or rejected (with a justification agreed by the HAZOP leader and the plant manager). The register in section 8 is the tracking list.
                • High scenarios whose protection relies on instrumented trips — the blocked discharge (TSHH-212/222), D-150 overfill (LSHH-150 through V100), loss of suction (LSLL-200 on the shared LI-200) — go to LOPA to decide whether the trips are enough or a new SIF (low-flow trip, overfill protection) is needed (IEC 61511). See the Safety layers and LOPA tabs.
                • The Rev C options (casing pressure transmitters with PAH on the idle pump, MOV discharge valves interlocked with the motors) answer R18 and R19; putting them in service is a change and goes through management of change, which checks whether this HAZOP must be updated.
                • Revalidate the HAZOP periodically (typically every five years) and after incidents or near misses.
                • Use the simulator to train operators on the scenarios this HAZOP found and to time their response against the D-150 hold-up (R33).

                Safety layers · layers of protection for the feed pump station

                Teaching slide deck · Safety layers — the six layers on the pump-station P&ID, the pump trips and their cause-and-effect matrix, the operating window, independence of the trips, thermal relief and containment of a gas-oil pump station.
                Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

                Safety must cover failures of equipment (including control) and of people, and more than one failure at a time. The response should be limited, keeping production where possible. So protection is built in layers, each independent of the others, with more strength held in reserve as the event gets more serious. Source: course 2105625 Process Safety (safety hierarchy), applied to the cat-cracker feed pumps P-200A/B. Settings come from the model (K) and the page's alarm table; values marked "assumed" are for teaching.

                1 The six layers · 2 P&ID layer by layer · 3 What each layer does · SIS cause-and-effect · 4 Integrity operating window · 5 Independence check · 6 Good practices · 7 Standards

                1 · The six layers

                LayerJob on the pump stationAutomatic?Needs power / computer?Needs a person?
                1 BPCSHolds the feed the cat cracker asks for (FRC-100 → V100), refuses unsafe pump startsYesYesSupervises; starts the spare
                2 AlarmsBring a lost flow, a hot casing, a level or a tripped motor to a personNo actionYesYes: decides
                3 SISStop a pump before it runs dry or cooks its seal; close V100 before D-150 overfillsYesYes (de-energise to trip: a power loss stops the motors)No (reset only)
                4 ReliefThermal relief of blocked-in liquid, the E-100 shell, the T200 ventYes, self-actuatingNoNo
                5 ContainmentKeep leaked gas oil in a bund, a kerb, a drip pan or a closed drain; isolate the tankPassive or remoteMostly noPartly
                6 Emergency responseFire water, foam, detection, evacuation, first aidNoPartlyYes

                Layers 1–3 need electrical power, computing and communication, so one power or computer failure could take out all three at once; that is why the trips de-energise to act and the valves go to a fail position, and relief, containment and emergency response are kept in reserve. On this station the safe state of the pumps (stopped) and the fail position of V100 (closed) do not agree: an air failure closes V100 while the running pump keeps going (section 5). Click a ring to open that layer on the P&ID.

                SIS and motor-protection cause-and-effect matrix (layer 3), live

                Effects read from bmsTrip(), motorTrip(), stopPump(), bmsStep() and step() in the model. "ACTIVE" = the condition of tripConditions(sim) is true now; "FIRST-OUT" = the cause latched in sim.P.sis.first (after a unit trip the low-level condition clears because no pump runs, so the first-out is what stays); "TRIPPED" = the motor trip latched in sim.P.sis.mt with its reason; "LATCHED" = LSHH-150 holding V100 shut.

                4 · Integrity operating window

                Each key variable has a target, alarm limits that still leave time to act, a trip, and a critical limit where damage comes quickly. The arrow is the live value: load a training exercise and watch it climb through the layers. Critical limits that are not in the design data are marked "assumed". The NPSH margin has no alarm and no trip at all in rev A — only the recommended suction-pressure alarm.

                5 · Independence check

                A layer must not share its sensor, logic or final element with the layer below, or one failure defeats both. The SIS column says which measurement tripConditions() actually reads — the drawing alone can mislead. An alarm that is the pre-alarm of a trip may share the trip's sensor, but LOPA then credits only one of them.

                7 · Standards

                • IEC 61511 / ISA-84: SIS life cycle, safety requirements specification (the C&E above), independence, SIL, proof testing. CCPS Layer of Protection Analysis and Guidelines for Safe Automation of Chemical Processes.
                • ISA-18.2 / EEMUA 191: alarm philosophy, priorities, rationalisation, suppression by operating state, alarm rates.
                • API 610 (centrifugal pumps: minimum continuous flow, reverse rotation, casing rated for the maximum discharge pressure) and API 682 (shaft seals, dual seals with leak detection).
                • API 520 / API 521 and ASME VIII Div. 1: relief sizing and installation — blocked outlet, control-valve failure, tube rupture, thermal expansion of blocked-in liquid.
                • API 2000 (venting of atmospheric storage tanks) and API 2350 (overfill protection of storage tanks).
                • NFPA 30 (flammable and combustible liquids: tank spacing, bunds, pump areas), NFPA 11 (foam) and NFPA 15 / 72 (water spray, fire alarm); the owner's emergency response plan.
                • Thai Department of Industrial Works: regulation on hazard identification, risk assessment and risk management plans (B.E. 2543) and the rules for storage and handling of hazardous and flammable substances in factories.

                Part A · Reliability for safety

                A1 · Definitions

                TermMeaningOn the pump station
                HazardInherent physical or chemical characteristic that can harm people, environment or property (CCPS)Gas oil above its flash point at the pumps and in E-100; m³ of it in T200 behind the pumps; a centrifugal pump that turns all its power into heat when nothing flows
                Hazardous eventRelease of material or energy that can cause harmSeal failure and a gas-oil fire at the pump slab; D-150 overfilled into the cat-cracker vent; hot oil flowing back into T200
                RiskRisk = consequence × frequencyA pump-slab fire with permanent injury (severity 4) tolerable only below 10−3 /yr (course criteria)
                Tolerable / residual riskRisk accepted in context / risk left after protectionThe LOPA target frequency / the mitigated frequency of the worksheet
                Reliability R(t)Probability of success during an interval of timeThe P-200A motor contactor still able to open at the end of a one-year proof-test interval
                PFDProbability of failure on demand; F(t) = 1 − R(t)The chance that TSHH-212 does not stop a deadheaded pump
                Deterministic / probabilistic analysisCan the design keep events within limits / what is the numerical risk and is it tolerablePiping rated for the shut-off head (no PSV needed for a blocked discharge) / LOPA below

                Is 99.9 % reliability good enough? The station starts a pump about once a month; a 1-in-1000 chance of starting it unvented is small, but the cat-cracker charge pump stops about twice a year, and every stop is a demand on the D-150 overfill protection and, through it, on the deadhead protection of P-200A. Safety needs both plant reliability (business continuity) and safety reliability (hazard prevention and mitigation).

                A2 · Failure rate from a population

                λ = ΔNf / (Ns · Δt): failures in the interval divided by the survivors and the interval length. 100 identical units (think of 100 mechanical seals in a refinery's pump population) are drawn from a Weibull life model R(t) = e−(t/α)β at the quantiles ti = α(−ln(1 − (i − 0.5)/100))1/β, shuffled with a seeded generator so the picture is stable. β < 1 is burn-in (a seal fitted wrongly fails early), β = 1 the useful life (constant λ = 1/α, the exponential model), β > 1 wear-out (faces and elastomers age).

                A3 · R(t), PFD and proof testing

                With a constant failure rate R(t) = e−λt and PFD(t) = F(t) = 1 − e−λt ≈ λt when PFD ≪ 0.1. A standby safeguard such as a motor contactor that has not opened for months fails unseen (welded contacts), so its PFD grows until the next proof test restores it: PFDavg = (1/T)∫0T(1 − e−λt)dt = 1 − (1 − e−λT)/(λT) ≈ λT/2. MTTF = ∫R dt = 1/λ.

                SIL (IEC 61511, demand mode)PFDavgRRF
                SIL 110−2 – 10−110 – 100
                SIL 210−3 – 10−2100 – 1 000
                SIL 310−4 – 10−31 000 – 10 000

                A4 · Reliability block diagrams and the station SIFs

Improving reliability: diversity (an under-power relay and a level trip see a dry-running pump by different physics), separation (an own transmitter and an own shut-off valve), fail-safe design (de-energise to trip: a lost supply stops the motors).

                Part B · Layers of protection analysis (LOPA)

                B1 · The method

                1. Take a scenario from the HAZOP (cause → consequence) and rate its severity; the severity sets the target frequency.
                2. Estimate the initiating event frequency (IEF) from failure data. If several causes lead to the same consequence, work each and add the frequencies.
                3. Credit each independent protection layer (IPL) with its PFD. A layer that shares a component with the initiating event, or with another credited layer, gets no credit; an alarm needs time — the model runs (B6) show whether the operator has 10 minutes.
                4. Apply enabling events (a check valve that happens to be passing) and conditional modifiers (probability of ignition, free water in the tank).
                5. Compare with the target: RRF = f / target. If RRF > 1 the gap sets the PFD, and so the SIL, of the extra layer.

                Lecture example: pressure control malfunction 0.1 /yr × high-pressure alarm 0.1 × relief valve 0.01 × occupancy 0.1 = /yr against a fatality target of 10−6 /yr → RRF = , not acceptable.

                B2 · Criteria used here (course risk matrix)

                SeverityTarget risk frequency (/yr)Health and safetyEnvironmentEconomic

                Likelihood levels by frequency: 5 most likely (~10 /yr), 4 likely (~1), 3 possible (~0.1), 2 rare (~0.01), 1 almost impossible (~0.001); the band boundaries are taken halfway between decades (on a log scale). Risk = severity × likelihood: 1 negligible, 2–6 low, 8–12 medium, 15–20 high, 25 extreme. Target frequencies differ by country (for a fatality about 10−4 to 10−6 /yr). This matrix is stricter than the HAZOP tab's S × L banding, which was used only to rank rows; the HAZOP severity scale (S3 = cat cracker loses its feed, S4 = gas-oil fire at the pumps or the tank) maps onto the course levels used below.

                B3 · What counts as an IPL

                An IPL must be independent of the initiating event and of the other credited layers, specific to the scenario, dependable (its PFD can be justified — including the time to act: an alarm needs ≥ 10 min between alarm and harm) and auditable (tested). Procedures, training and inspection are safeguards but usually not IPLs; a check valve is an enabling condition, not an IPL. On this station one motor contactor earns one credit, however many trips drive it, and an alarm that shares its element with a trip (TIAH-212 / TSHH-212, LIAL-200 / LSLL-200, LIAH-150 / LSHH-150) is credited only when the trip is not.

                  Part C · Bow-tie

                  A bow-tie is several LOPAs drawn around one top event (the moment control of the hazard is lost). Threats on the left pass prevention barriers; consequences on the right sit behind mitigation (recovery) barriers and conditional modifiers. Escalation factors are conditions that defeat a barrier (a shared transmitter that sticks, a detector out of calibration, a supply lost in the same dip). The top-event frequency is the sum of the threat frequencies times their barrier PFDs; a threat marked "LOPA Lx" starts from the sum of that scenario's initiating events. Barrier colours follow the Safety layers tab; grey is design, a check valve or a conditional modifier. Click a barrier to fail it. The bow-tie does not apply the LOPA independence rules, so read it as a picture of the layers, and the worksheet as the number.

                  Two times decide whether a SIF is fast enough. The process safety time (PST) runs from the moment the process crosses the trip point to the moment the hazardous event happens if nothing acts; the response time runs from the same moment to the moment the station is in its safe state (sensor, logic scan, trip delay, contactor or valve, and the coast-down of the pump). Good practice asks for a response no longer than half the PST. The PST belongs to a demand, not to a trip: the same trip can have hours for one cause and no time at all for another, which is why each card below lists every demand the model can run.

                    1 What a C&E diagram is · 2 The diagram · 3 How to read a row · 4 Notes · 5 Checks against the simulator

                    1 · What a cause and effect diagram is

                    • A cause is one sensed condition with its direction and setting (low, low-low, high, high-high, push-button). Alarm-only causes put a message on the DCS alarm list and sound the horn; trip causes act on motors, valves and latches and raise a trip alarm.
                    • An effect is one action on one device or latch, written as a code in the Trip Action row (STOP a motor, C close a valve, TP trip and latch, F first-out, A activate, P permissive, RB reset blocked). A mark in the matrix says which causes drive it; R marks an action that exists only with the Rev C MOV interlock.
                    • On a pump station the protections are of three kinds, and the matrix shows them side by side: the unit trip (LSLL-200, ESD) stops both pumps and latches a first-out; the motor protection (TSHH-212/222, overload relays 49-210/220) stops one motor and latches only that motor; the D-150 high-high acts on the feed valve, not on the pumps.
                    • The matrix follows the SRS of each SIF (SRS of SIF tab, document PPS-V1-IN-SRS-001) and the alarm list, and must match the logic exactly. Here the effects are read from the simulator's trip functions and section 5 tests every row on copies of the model.

                          5a · Deadhead: how long a pump survives against a closed valve

                          Minimum flow. With V100 held at small openings (FRC-100 in MAN, 10 minutes each) the casing stays cool at a fraction of a litre per second — the heat goes out with the liquid — but the pump runs rough: the model's vibration rises well before the casing warms. The minimum continuous flow of a centrifugal pump is set by recirculation and vibration (typically 25–45 % of the best-efficiency flow), not by heating.

                          6 · Load following: the cat cracker sets the rate

                          FRC-100's set point is the cat cracker's remote set point, so the station follows its charge. Here the cat cracker cuts its charge in one step at t = 1 min, and FRC-100's set point follows either in the same step or as a ramp. A ramp that lags the charge leaves the difference in D-150; a step moves the preheater duty suddenly. Pick a run:

                            Process reliability · how often the cat cracker loses its feed, and how to make that rarer

                            Teaching slide deck — reliability, failure rate and availability, series / parallel / standby / k-of-N structures, the manual spare against the D-150 ride-through window, the feed station as a series system, dormant failures of the spare, inventory, maintenance and life-cycle cost, all on the pump-station model.
