                            Follows the course material on reliability (T. Marlin, Operability in Process Design, Ch. 4 Reliability; the Introduction to Reliability Engineering course: failure statistics, MTTF/MTBF, series/parallel/k-of-N, critical items). This tab is about the reliability of production: an interruption of the feed costs cat-cracker charge and money. The reliability of safeguards (probability of failure on demand of LSLL-200, TSHH-212/222, LSHH-150 and the motor protection) is on the LOPA tab. Failure rates are the course's generic all-modes values or assumed values; every fraction, repair time, response time and capital cost marked assumed is a teaching value. Numbers marked model come from runs of this simulator on copies of the design state (never the live plant); lost charge is priced at the page's training price PRICE.short.

                            1 Definitions · 2 Failure rate and life · 3 Structures · 4 The manual spare and the D-150 window · 5 The station as a series system · 6 Dormant failures of the spare · 7 Design for reliability · 8 Operating near the best-efficiency point · 9 Inventory: D-150 and T200 · 10 Maintenance · 11 Life-cycle cost · 12 Pump-station reliability audit

                            1 · Reliability, availability and why they differ

                            Availability is not reliability. A feed station that stops eight times a year but is back within five minutes each time shows 99.99 % availability and poor reliability: each stop is a cat-cracker upset, a hot slug of oil from E-100 and a start of a cold spare. Reliability counts the events, availability counts the time.

                            2 · Failure rate, the bathtub and the exponential model

                            Failure rate λ(t) = failures per unit time ÷ items still working. Over a life it often follows the bathtub: infant mortality (falling λ), chance failures (constant λ), wear-out (rising λ). Most equipment does not show the full bathtub (the RCM studies found six patterns, most without wear-out), so the right maintenance depends on the pattern. With constant λ:

                            R(t) = e−λt,  F(t) = 1 − R(t),  MTTF = 1/λ

                            Weibull: R(t) = exp[−(t/η)β], λ(t) = (β/η)(t/η)β−1. Move β through 1 to see the three regions of the bathtub.

                            3 · Structures: series, parallel, standby, k out of N

                            A plant is many components joined in structures; the structure sets the system reliability. The formulas assume independent failures (no common cause) and, for standby, a perfect switch.

                            4 · The standby lesson for this unit: P-200B is a manual-start spare

                            The standby formula assumes a perfect, instant switch. P-200B is lined up and primed, but an operator starts it. Whether that is good enough depends on how long the consumer can ride through the gap. Here the consumer is the cat cracker, and its ride-through is the inventory of D-150: at the design level , the drum holds above LALL-150 ( %), which trips the cat-cracker charge pump. With no feed and the cat cracker drawing , the window is V/Q = . The model runs below trip P-200A on the design state and start P-200B Δ later (ppRun, levels free, SIS on, scripted at actions).

                            The window depends on where D-150 sits

                            A person as the switch

                            Hearing the alarm, recognising a pump trip and starting P-200B from the console is a human response with a spread. Take it as lognormal (assumed; set its median and spread). The window is the model's, at the D-150 level you choose:

                            5 · The station as a series system: what interrupts the feed, and what reaches the cat cracker

                            For production every element in the chain tank → suction → running pump → V100 → E-100 → D-150 must work, so the station is a series system for feed interruptions: λsys = Σ λi fi, where fi is the fraction of element i's failures (all modes) that stops the feed. Only part of those interruptions reach the cat cracker: the feed must stay off longer than the D-150 window w. For an element whose restoration is a repair with mean τ (exponential), that chance is e−w/τ (the inventory formula of part 9); for an operator action it is the miss probability of part 4; for the running pump it is the spare not running in time or not able to run (fail to start , assumed, plus the dormant unavailability of part 6). A lost charge costs the downtime plus for the cat cracker to re-establish its charge (assumed), priced at .

                            6 · Dormant failures: a spare that is not ready is found only when it is needed

                            A running pump announces its failures (current, flow, noise). A spare that stands still does not: air left in the casing after maintenance, a seized bearing, a starter fault or a closed valve stay hidden until the next demand, a test run or a routine changeover. With dormant faults arriving at rate λd and a test every T, the spare is unavailable for a mean fraction q ≈ λdT/2 of the time (exact: 1 − (1 − e−λT)/(λT)). The changeover A ↔ B is the test of the motor, the prime and the bearings.

                            The check valve on the idle pump is the classic dormant failure of a parallel station. It does nothing visible while it holds; when it passes, it neither trips nor alarms by itself and it is revealed only by a test of the idle leg or by its local gauge on rounds. Its cost is lost capacity for as long as it stays undetected, so the test interval matters as much as for the spare's motor. Continuous monitoring of the idle casing (the Rev C option on the SIS tab) turns it from a dormant into a revealed failure.

                            7 · Design for reliability

                            "There is no safe side in equipment sizing." An oversized pump runs left of its best-efficiency point: recirculation, vibration, seal and bearing failures ("pumps don't die; engineers kill them"). An undersized one runs out at the end of its curve with no margin. Match the equipment to its service; spare the items that fail often; give every single point of failure a by-pass, a switchable twin or at least a fast repair.

                            8 · Operating for reliability: stay near the best-efficiency point

                            Seal and bearing life fall away from the best-efficiency flow: at low flow the impeller recirculates and the radial thrust grows; at runout the NPSH margin and the thrust go the other way. The life curve below is an assumed teaching curve with the usual shape (flat across about 80–110 % of BEP, half the life at 50 %, floor 10 %); the points on it are this station's own operating states from the model (one pump at several FRC-100 set points, and both pumps sharing 14 L/s). The model's own vibration term rises below 45 % of the design flow, which is the same message from the simulator.

                            9 · Reliability through inventory: D-150 after the station, T200 before it

                            A tank between an unreliable unit and the next one lets the next unit run while the first is repaired. With the upstream repair time exponential (mean MTTR) and a holdup τ = V/F, the chance that one outage is covered is 1 − e−τ/MTTR, so Rsys = R₂[R₁ + (1 − R₁)(1 − e−τ/MTTR)]. This station has two such buffers: D-150 protects the cat cracker from the pumps (minutes), T200 protects the pumps from the tank farm (hours: ).

                            The same buffer must be refilled after it has been used. A spare started late leaves D-150 near LALL-150, and with the cat cracker drawing 14 L/s only the pump's margin above 14 L/s refills it: A second interruption before then finds no window. Inventory also has a price: tank cost, a larger hydrocarbon inventory, and hot oil standing in the drum.

                            10 · Maintenance for reliability

                            11 · Life-cycle cost: how many pumps?

                            Life-cycle costing adds the costs that reliability changes: capital and maintenance of the extra pumps, how often the cat cracker loses its charge and for how long. One pump means every pump failure stops the feed for the whole repair; a second pump turns most of them into a changeover inside the D-150 window; a third can still be started inside the same window when the second will not run (unlike a fired heater, where the window is seconds). The spare's readiness comes from part 6 (test interval) and the operator from part 4. Prices and pump costs are assumed; the cost of lost charge is PRICE.short.

                            12 · Pump-station reliability audit

                            The checks a reliability engineer makes on a pump station before failures occur, with this model's numbers (all model runs on copies of the design state with ppRun; alarm limits from the page's ALM, trip limits from K).

                            1 Efficiency and priorities · 2 The station now · 3 Throttling against variable speed · 4 Which pump, and how many · 5 Strainer fouling · 6 E-100 steam · 7 Options sized for the unit · 8 Pushing toward the constraint · 9 Key energy variables (live)

                            1 · Efficiency, optimisation and their place among the priorities

                            Efficiency (in operation the same as optimisation) is good economic performance: the feed delivered at the rate and temperature the cat cracker asks for, with less electricity, less steam and no lost charge. For energy, efficiency = useful output ÷ total input, and a chain of steps multiplies: the lecture's boiler 90 % × turbo-generator 40 % × transmission 90 % = 32.4 %.

                            Four ways to get it (lecture): design with the right capacities; use the equipment in the most efficient way; choose better structures (speed control instead of a throttle, heat recovery); choose the best operating conditions inside the window. Efficiency is the sixth priority: it never overrides safety, the environment, equipment protection, a smooth rate or the feed temperature the cat cracker needs.

                            Efficiencies multiply along the chain — and the money is not where the kilowatts are

                            2 · The station now: direct efficiency and where the electricity goes

                            Direct method for the running pump: ηpump = hydraulic power ρ g Q ΔH ÷ shaft power. For the station, wire-to-water efficiency = useful hydraulic power ÷ electric power, where the useful head is the static lift (D-150 pressure and height above the T200 level) plus the line friction the feed must overcome (suction line and strainer, pump legs, line and E-100), and the throttling head across V100 is counted as a loss. Computed live from DCS readings only, the way an energy engineer would: flow from FT-100, shaft power from the motor current II-210/220 (inverse of the motor's current line), V100 from the FRC-100 output, T200 level from LI-200, heads from the healthy system curve. When the equipment is healthy the estimate equals the model's truth; when it is not, the estimate drifts — which is why the number is worth trending.

                            3 · Design with the right capacity: throttling against variable speed

                            A constant-speed pump reaches a lower flow only by burning head in a control valve. A variable-speed drive (VSD) lowers the pump curve instead: by the affinity laws flow ∝ speed, head ∝ speed², power ∝ speed³. The fixed-speed curve below is the model (FRC-100 AUTO at each set point, P-200A); the VSD curves keep V100 at a fixed opening (the same system curve) and find the speed with nomNet, with the model's power line scaled by s³ and s² (and an assumed drive efficiency of ). The rule of thumb "power ∝ speed³ ∝ flow³" is drawn too.

                            4 · Use the equipment well: which pump, and how many

                            P-200B has the higher shut-off head (). Which is cheaper to run at 14 L/s? And what does a second pump cost when one would do, or when one is not enough? Model runs, FRC-100 AUTO at the set point, levels held, 300 s:

                            5 · Strainer fouling: what it costs, and what it does not

                            A plugging suction strainer multiplies the suction-line loss (the model's fault scales the strainer loss up to 8 ×). Rule of thumb heard on many plants: "a dirty strainer wastes pump energy". Model sweep at FRC-100 14 L/s and, for the capacity, with V100 wide open:

                            6 · E-100: steam per tonne of feed

                            E-100 condenses steam on the shell to heat the feed from to about 150 °C. Its specific consumption is the key energy number of the station: . Rule of thumb: the duty is ρ cp Q (Tout − Tin), so each °C of outlet costs 1/(Tout − Tin) of the steam. Model runs with TIC-110 in AUTO at each target (14 L/s, 3600 s):

                            Fouling: steam, and the room to heat

                            TIC-110 in MAN against AUTO when the rate changes

                            7 · Options sized for this unit

                            Each option at the prices you set (initialised from the page's training prices). Savings come from the model sweeps above; capital costs are assumed teaching values. Electricity is cheap here and steam is not: compare the last column before choosing.

                            8 · Best operating conditions: push toward the constraint, but only as far as the variability allows

                            Many conditions do not affect safety or quality but do affect profit; the best value usually sits against a constraint, and how close you can go depends on variability (the lecture's cracking furnace; the fired heater's O₂ set point against CO). With a VSD the energy optimum is to run V100 as far open as possible with the least pump head: lower speed, less throttling. The constraint is the flow the cat cracker may ask for: with V100 at 100 % there is no room left to answer a higher demand. Take the demand as normal around 14 L/s with spread σ (assumed); the feed is short when the demand exceeds the most the pump gives at that speed, P = ½ erfc[(Qmax − 14)/(σ√2)]. Computed live with nomNet (P-200A, T200 at its design level).

                            Industrial practice: reduce the variability first (a steadier cat-cracker demand, a valve-position controller that trims the speed slowly to keep V100 near a target such as 90 %), then move the target; keep a way back to full speed when the demand rises. On this station the prize is small (part 7), so the same logic is worth more on E-100's outlet temperature.

                            9 · Energy monitoring: key energy variables of the station (live)

                            A plant energy dashboard tracks the specific consumption (energy per unit of product) against its benchmark and the key energy variables (KEV) that move it. Benchmarks are the design point (model, computed the same way from its DCS readings); alarm limits come from ALM. Read only, refreshed every second.

Marlin, Process Operability class materials; US DOE, Improving Pumping System Performance: A Sourcebook for Industry (affinity laws, throttling, VSD); US DOE, Improving Steam System Performance (insulation, steam cost).

                            1 What an SOP is · 2 Format · 3 SOP register · 4 SOP viewer · 5 Writing rules · 6 Life of an SOP

                            1 · What an SOP is, and which activities need one

                            A standard operating procedure is the written, approved way to carry out one task: the same steps, in the same order, with the same checks, whoever is on shift. It turns the reasons worked out on the other tabs — the start-up order, the permissives, the operating limits, the trips — into actions an operator can follow at 3 a.m. under pressure.

                            A pump station looks simple, but most of its incidents happen in transitions done from memory: a pump started without venting, a wrong valve closed during a change-over, steam left on a stopped feed. The scripted cold start-up on the Transition operation tab needs about fifteen operator actions in a fixed order, split between the board and the field. The US process safety management standard lists what must be written down; the Thai Ministry of Industry notification on process safety management asks for written operating procedures in the same way.

                            6 · The life of an SOP

                            Draft from the design intent and the hazard studies (HAZOP, LOPA) → verify on the simulator (the graded procedures run the same steps against the model) → review by operations, process and safety → approve and train → use, with deviations reported → review after any change (management of change: a new pump, a new trip setting, a different feed), after an incident, or at a fixed interval (typically 1–3 years; OSHA asks for annual certification that procedures are current).

                            Work through Parts A to G in order. Record your answers and evidence (screenshots, CSV files) as you go.

                            1 Purpose · 2 The unit · 3 Control scheme · 4 Safety systems · 5 Operating rules · 6 Activities A–G · 7 Grading · 8 Report checklist

                            1 · Purpose

                            A pair of identical centrifugal pumps in parallel is the most common piece of rotating equipment in a plant. By the end you should be able to:

                            1. Read the P&ID and the DCS, and state the normal value and alarm limits of every key tag.
                            2. Explain a pump curve, a system curve and the operating point, and predict the flow when V100, the static head, the speed or the number of pumps changes.
                            3. Start up, change over and shut down a centrifugal pump safely: prime and vent, start against a closed discharge, confirm shut-off head, never run it dry or deadheaded.
                            4. Use local gauges and the pump curve to tell a weak pump from flow that goes somewhere else, extra resistance, cavitation or a wrong meter.
                            5. Troubleshoot with the six stages of a systematic method, and propose a change that stops a fault recurring.

                            2 · The unit

                            Cat-cracker feed (gas oil, 60 °C) is drawn from cone-roof tank T200 through the common suction valve V200 and strainer S-200. Pump A (P-200A: suction V202, local gauge PI-210, check valve NRV-210, discharge V201) usually runs; pump B (P-200B: V206, PI-220, NRV-220, V205) is the identical spare. Both were uprated four years ago from 1800 to 3600 rpm with 10 kW motors. The legs join one discharge header; FRC-100 measures the flow at FE-100 and moves V100 (fail closed) to hold the cat cracker's remote set point of 14 L/s. Steam preheater E-100 heats the feed to about 150 °C (TIC-110, normally in MAN) and it runs into the cat-cracker feed drum D-150.

                            The design flow (14 L/s), the speed and motor size, the shut-off heads (A 45.0 m, B 46.5 m) and the gauge readings with B running (PI-220 34 m, idle PI-210 0.5 m, V100 output ≈ 80 %) come from the troubleshooting case this OTS is built on. The fluid properties, tank size, suction losses, delivery static head (24 m), preheater, D-150 and the cat cracker's charge are engineering assumptions chosen so that the model reproduces those readings.

                            4 · Safety systems

                            Alarm limits

                            5 · Operating rules

                            1. Never start a pump dry. Suction open, casing vented until liquid shows, vent closed.
                            2. Start against a closed (or just cracked) discharge valve, confirm shut-off head on the local gauge, then open the discharge within 2 minutes. A centrifugal pump at zero flow heats its casing.
                            3. Never start a pump whose shaft is turning backwards.
                            4. Keep the idle pump's discharge valve closed unless the procedure says otherwise: the check valve alone is not a barrier you can see.
                            5. Never throttle a suction valve; if the flow must be cut, cut it with V100.
                            6. Steam only on moving oil: cut TV-110 before the flow stops, open it after the flow is established.
                            7. Read both local gauges whenever the flow is short with V100 at 100 %, and compare with the pump curve before opening anything up.

                            Part B · Pump and system curves

                              The process · cat-cracker feed pumps in parallel

                              1 Principles · 2 Block flow diagram · 3 Process description · 4 What each unit does · 5 Steady state: streams · 6 Steady state: units · 7 Balances · 8 Key relationships

                              Tables marked now are live from the simulator; design is the lined-out design point with noise off.

                              1 · Principles of the process

                              • What a centrifugal pump does. The impeller spins the liquid and throws it outward; the volute slows it and turns the velocity into pressure. It adds head, not pressure: H = Δp / (ρ·g). The same pump gives the same metres of head to any thin liquid; the gauges on this unit are read in metres of liquid (1 m ≈ 8.5 kPa for this oil).
                              • The pump curve. Head falls as flow rises: here ΔH = H₀·(N/3600)² − k·Q², with H₀ = 45.0 m for A and 46.5 m for B (shut-off heads measured on test) and k = 0.0663 m/(L/s)². Shut-off head is the most a pump can ever make.
                              • The system curve. What the pipework asks for: Hsys = Hstatic + K(x)·Q². The static part (20 m here: 24 m delivery minus the 4 m of liquid above the pump) is paid at any flow; the friction part grows with Q². Closing V100 raises K and steepens the curve.
                              • The operating point is where the two curves cross. A control valve can only move the point along the pump curve; at 100 % open it has nothing left, and the flow is set by the pump.
                              • Affinity laws. For the same pump at a new speed N: Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³. The 1750-rpm vendor data (7 L/s, 12 m shut-off, 1 kW) scale to about 14.4 L/s, 50.8 m and 8.7 kW at 3600 rpm.
                              • Parallel pumps. At the same header head their flows add. Because the system curve has a large static part, a second pump in parallel raises the header head and each pump runs further back on its curve: two pumps give much less than twice the flow.
                              • Check valves and the idle pump. The idle pump is joined to the live header only through its check valve and its discharge block valve. If the check valve passes, header liquid flows back through the idle pump to the suction (driving it backwards like a turbine); the running pump must supply process + back-flow, runs further out on its curve at lower head, and less reaches the meter.
                              • Accountability. Around the pumps and header nothing is created: Qpump = Qprocess + Qelsewhere. A low reading on FRC-100 has three homes: the pump makes less, flow goes elsewhere, or the reading is wrong.
                              • Power. P = ρ·g·Q·H / η; this pump needs about 2.3 kW at shut-off and 5.7 kW at 14 L/s (η ≈ 70 %). The motor current follows the power, so the ammeter is a cheap witness: more flow → more amps.
                              • NPSH. To avoid cavitation the suction must offer more head above vapour pressure than the pump needs: NPSHa = (ps − pv)/(ρ·g) ≥ NPSHr. NPSHr rises with Q² (about 4.5 m at 14 L/s here). A plugged strainer, a low tank or light ends in the feed eat into the margin.
                              • Minimum flow and priming. At zero flow all the shaft power goes into the trapped liquid: the casing heats (here about 6 °C per minute). A pump that is not full of liquid makes almost no head and wrecks its seal within a minute.

                              2 · Block flow diagram

                              Numbered circles are the streams of section 5. Blue = feed, red = steam, teal = condensate, purple dashed = back-flow path through an idle pump (zero at design).

                              3 · Process description

                              1. Storage and suction (streams 1, 2). The tank farm tops up T200 through HIC-199 (14 L/s at design, 30 % level). The feed leaves through V200 and the strainer S-200 into a common suction header. With 4 m of liquid above the pumps and 3.5 m of suction loss at 14 L/s, the suction gauge PI-209 reads about 0.5 m.
                              2. Pumps (streams 3, 4). Pump A runs: at 14 L/s it makes about 32 m of head (PI-210 ≈ 32.4 m) and draws about 13 A. Pump B stands by with V206 and V205 open, its casing at suction head (PI-220 ≈ 0.5 m) and its check valve NRV-220 holding the header back.
                              3. Header and flow control (streams 5, 6). FE-100 measures the flow; FRC-100 holds the cat cracker's remote set point (14 L/s) with V100 about 84 % open on pump A (about 80 % on the stronger pump B). The low-point drain on the header is normally closed.
                              4. Preheat (streams 7, 9, 10). E-100 condenses about 4 t/h of steam at about 5 bar g to heat the feed from 60 to 150 °C (2.3 MW). TIC-110 is normally in MAN: the steam valve stays where it is, so a smaller feed comes out hotter.
                              5. Feed drum and cat cracker (stream 8). D-150 (30 m³) buffers the feed; the cat cracker draws 14 L/s. When the feed is short, D-150 falls at the difference (about 34 % per hour for a 2.8 L/s shortfall).
                              6. Protection. LSLL-200 stops both pumps before T200 runs dry; TSHH-212/222 and the overload relays stop a pump that is deadheaded, dry or overloaded; LSHH-150 closes V100 before D-150 overfills; V100 and TV-110 fail closed.

                              How to use the curves

                              1. Find the flow: the pump runs where its curve meets the system curve. Close V100 → the red curve steepens → the point moves left and up.
                              2. Check the meter: read the running pump's local gauge (and PI-209). Its head on the curve gives the flow the pump is really making. If that is well above FRC-100, flow is going somewhere else (idle leg, drain) or the meter reads low.
                              3. Check the pump: close its discharge valve for less than a minute and read shut-off head. Low shut-off = worn, blocked, wrong speed or rotation.
                              4. Parallel pumps: with a large static head, the second pump adds little flow unless the valve opens.
                              5. Speed: half the speed gives a quarter of the head: at 1800 rpm neither pump can lift the 20 m static head at useful flow.
